papers.title: Efficient preparation of fatty acid methyl esters using liquid lipase from thermotolerant fungus Rasamsonia emersonii via synergistic strategies.
papers.abstractText: Lipase-catalyzed biodiesel preparation in non-aqueous media has the advantages of reduced energy consumption, simplified recovery of fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs), and minimized environment pollution, etc. To discover a novel thermophilic lipase, achieve its high-level expression, and develop it as an efficient liquid biocatalyst for FAMEs production via methanolysis of plant oils in non-aqueous media, a lipase gene from the thermophilic fungus Rasamsonia emersonii was cloned and efficiently expressed through synergistic strategies including computational codon optimization and increased gene dosage in the host genome. The resulting liquid lipase preparation was directly employed as a biocatalyst for FAMEs production. Under optimized reaction conditions, a conversion rate of approximately 95% was achieved. This study provides a feasible approach for the large-scale production of thermophilic lipase. The strategy of directly using of liquid lipase as a biocatalyst for FAMEs preparation substantially simplifies enzyme immobilization, regeneration, and product recovery processes, offering an efficient alternative for enzymatic FAMEs production.

papers.title: Enhanced Rhizomucor miehei Lipase Production through Morphological and Fermentation Optimization in Aspergillus oryzae
papers.abstractText: Abstract       Rhizomucor miehei   lipase (RML) is widely applied in food processing, lipid modification, and biocatalysis; however, the scale-up of its heterologous production in Aspergillus oryzae (A. oryzae) is constrained by excessive mycelial aggregation, oxygen limitation, and unfavorable broth rheology. An integrated morphology and fermentation engineering strategy was developed to improve RML production in recombinant   A. oryzae   . First, at the shake-flask level, talc addition facilitated the formation of uniform pellets, with an optimal mean pellet diameter of approximately 0.7 mm and a maximum RML activity of 289.0 U/mL. Subsequently, a staged agitation program was established in a 5-L bioreactor fermentation to maintain the target pellet size, increasing RML activity to 486.5 U/mL, which was 70.7% higher than that of the control (285.0 U/mL). Comparative intracellular metabolite profiling showed that the optimized process was accompanied by increased levels of serine and threonine, which are the two most abundant amino acid residues in RML, together with glutamine. These metabolic changes suggested an improved supply of amino acid building blocks for protein biosynthesis and provided a possible metabolic explanation for the enhanced RML accumulation. Continuous feeding was introduced to sustain nutrient availability during the mid- to late-fermentation stages, thereby accelerating RML accumulation and increasing the final activity to 570.0 U/mL. Finally, late-stage pH control at 8.0 improved pellet stability and further enhanced RML production, yielding 742.0 U/mL, equivalent to 2.6-fold the control. Overall, this integrated strategy provides a practical framework for the bioreactor production of recombinant lipases by filamentous fungi.

papers.title: Recombinant thermotolerant alkaline lipase from Lysinibacillus fusiformis for detergent and hard (Ras) cheese applications: cloning, expression, molecular docking, and characterization.
papers.abstractText: Background Thermostable and alkaline lipases are of significant interest for industrial applications, particularly in detergents and food processing. This study aimed to isolate, clone, and express lipase-encoding genes from a potent bacterial source to produce a thermo-tolerant alkaline lipase with enhanced catalytic efficiency and practical applicability. Results Among several bacterial isolates, the most potent lipase producer was identified as Lysinibacillus fusiformis, and its 16 S rRNA sequence was deposited in GenBank (PP757498). Three lipase-encoding genes (est, est2, and lipA) were successfully isolated, cloned, and heterologously expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3). Their sequences were submitted to GenBank under accession numbers PX136937.1, PX136938.1, and PX136936.1, respectively. The recombinant lipase encoded by lipA (rLipase) exhibited the highest activity (150 U/mL) compared with the native enzyme (56.2 U/mL). Molecular docking analysis demonstrated strong binding affinity of rLipase toward major fatty acid derivatives in olive oil, with the highest affinity for linoleic acid (- 8.0 kcal/mol), followed by oleic acid (- 7.8 kcal/mol) and palmitic acid (- 7.3 kcal/mol). These interactions were stabilized by hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonding, with key contributions from critical amino acid residues, particularly VAL250. The partially purified recombinant lipase (rLipase) exhibited a maximum activity of 320 U/mL at 80 °C and pH 9, demonstrating remarkable thermostability and alkaline tolerance. Functional evaluation showed that rLipase improved the detergent efficiency for oil stain-removal from cotton fabrics. In addition, supplementation with 0.4% rLipase accelerated Ras cheese ripening by shortening the maturation period from 120 to 90 days with maintaining the desired ripening process. Conclusions The recombinant lipase from Lysinibacillus fusiformis demonstrated high thermal stability, alkaline tolerance, and strong catalytic efficiency. Its effectiveness in detergent formulations and cheese ripening highlights its potential as a versatile industrial biocatalyst for lipid bioconversion and related applications.

papers.title: Immobilization of Candida antarctica B lipase on polystyrene microspheres to synthesize oligomers from glycerol
papers.abstractText: Abstract    Glycerol can serve as a monomer for the production of polymers and oligomers through polycondensation reactions. These processes are catalyzed by heterogeneous biocatalysts. The study was divided into two parts: (i) preparing a heterogeneous biocatalyst based on Candida antarctica lipase and poly(styrene-co-divinylbenzene); and (ii) examining the polycondensation of glycerol with ethyl succinate mediated by the immobilized lipase. In these polycondensation reactions, oligomers with weight-average molecular masses (Mw) ranging from 346 to 759 g mol−1 were produced. The amount of glycerol (Gl) was the most significant factor influencing molecular weight (Mw) and the degree of polymerization (PD), showing a strong positive effect on polymer chain growth. A nonlinear relationship between Mw and catalyst concentration was observed, with Mw reaching its maximum at intermediate biocatalyst loadings. The linear effects of biocatalyst loading and reaction time on PD were not statistically significant. The biocatalyst was reused in four cycles with no notable loss of activity.

papers.title: Yarrowia lipolytica and Komagataella phaffii (Pichia pastoris) as Hosts for Heterologous Expression of Lipases.
papers.abstractText: The market for industrial lipases is growing due to their wide range of applications. To produce these recombinant enzymes to increase the productivity of the bioprocess, various cell factories, including yeast, have been selected. In the last two decades, the study and improvement of two nonconventional yeasts: K. phaffii and Y. lipolytica as cell factories for heterologous lipase production have increased. However, it is important to consider their differences when choosing between the two cell factories. This chapter compares the characteristics of these yeasts and explores options for enhancing the expression of heterologous lipases at both the molecular and bioprocess levels.

papers.title: What drives the cost of biowaste-to-lipase production? Linking titre, rate and yield to techno-economic performance in batch-to-continuous Pichia pastoris fermentation.
papers.abstractText: Fruit and vegetable (FV) waste represents an underutilized organic stream in Europe, yet its soluble sugar fraction remains poorly exploited as a bioprocess feedstock. Recombinant enzyme production from biowaste is often bottlenecked by heterogeneous substrate composition, low fermentable sugar titres, and uncertain process economics. This study evaluates the techno-economic feasibility of recombinant Candida rugosa lipase type 1 (CRL1) production in Pichia pastoris (Komagataella phaffii) under the constitutive glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase promoter pGAP across three carbon sources: commercial glucose (Scenario A), mechanically pressed fruit and vegetable juice (Scenario B), and an enzymatically hydrolysed, nanofiltered fruit and vegetablesugar stream (Scenario C). Bench-scale fermentation kinetics were integrated into 24 SuperPro Designer models across four scales (1 to 5000 L nominal vessel capacity; 0.75 to 3750 L working volume) under batch and continuous chemostat ([Formula: see text]) modes. Interpreted through the Titre, Rate, and Yield (TRY) framework, continuous operation on glucose increased volumetric CRL1 productivity 12.6-fold over batch (0.084 vs. 0.06 U L-1 h-1. Conversely, continuous operation on the hydrolysed stream did not improve productivity over batch, indicating potential kinetic inhibition from enzymatic pretreatment products or suboptimal dilution rate. At the 5000 L vessel scale under continuous mode, unit production costs were $1186, $36,049, and $3416 [Formula: see text] for Scenarios A, B, and C, respectively, all exceeding the commodity lipase benchmark ($25 [Formula: see text]). Facility-dependent costs dominated Scenarios A and B (73% and 78% of OPEX), whereas enzyme reagents dominated Scenario C (75%). Sensitivity analysis confirmed that secreted protein titre and downstream recovery efficiency are the primary economic drivers, demonstrating that feedstock acquisition cost is not the binding constraint. Early-stage TEA driven by bench-scale kinetic parameterization provides essential screening prior to pilot-scale investment in biowaste-to-enzyme biorefineries.

papers.title: Screening and Fermentation Parameter Optimization of Lipase-Producing Trichosporon asahii.
papers.abstractText: Waste cooking oil is generated in large quantities during food-waste processing, and its complex composition may pose environmental and public-health risks if it is improperly managed. Lipase-mediated conversion of waste cooking oil into biodiesel offers a promising strategy for both waste-oil valorization and greener fuel production. To expand the available microbial sources of lipases, this study isolated a strain with strong lipase-producing capacity from composted food-waste samples. The isolate was identified using molecular biological methods, the enzymatic properties of the extracellular lipase were characterized, and fermentation conditions for enzyme production were optimized by response surface methodology. The strain was identified as Trichosporon asahii. The lipase showed optimal catalytic activity at 40 °C and pH 8.0. Na+ and K+ enhanced lipase activity, whereas Ca2+, Mg2+, Mn2+, and Fe3+ inhibited the enzyme. Response surface optimization showed that a maximum lipase activity of 70.816 U/mL was obtained at a fermentation temperature of 31 °C, an initial pH of 6.33, an inoculum size of 6.843%, and a fermentation time of 120 h, representing an approximately 10-fold increase compared with the non-optimized condition. These findings provide a useful basis for developing food-waste-derived oils as biodiesel feedstocks through lipase-based fermentation and support the resource-oriented utilization of food waste.

papers.title: Isolation and Purification of Lipase From Soybean Sprouts for Biodiesel Production
papers.abstractText: Soybean (Glycine max) sprouts at various germination ages were evaluated as potential lipase sources for enzymatic production of biodiesel (FAME, fatty acid methyl esters). Lipase was extracted using phosphate buffer and partially purified through ammonium sulfate precipitation. Enzyme specific activity was quantified via the hydrolysis of p‐nitrophenyl palmitate. The purified lipase from 5‐day‐old sprouts exhibited the highest specific activity and catalyzed biodiesel synthesis with conversion yields of 47.8% for stearic acid and 63.0% for oleic acid, indicating a higher affinity toward unsaturated fatty acids. The successful formation of FAME was confirmed by thin‐layer chromatography and FTIR spectroscopy. These findings highlight soybean sprout‐derived lipase as a promising biocatalyst for sustainable biodiesel production.

papers.title: Porcine pancreas lipase: a versatile biocatalyst.
papers.abstractText: Porcine pancreatic lipase, a 1, 3-regioselective lipase, is one of the most widely used biocatalyst in academic as well as industrial processes. This lipase showed remarkable catalytic performance, often outclassed other types of lipases in producing valuable products through varieties of reactions. During hydrolysis of vegetable oil to fatty acid, mono and diacylglycerol, porcine pancreas lipase outclassed Candia rugosa and Thermomyces lanuginosus lipase. Porcine pancreas lipase efficiently catalyzed transesterification of vegetable oil to biodiesel as well. This lipase catalyzed esterification of organic acid and alcohol, glycerol and fatty acid, sugar and fatty acid resulting in organic ester, monoacylglycerol and sugar and fatty acid ester, respectively; outperformed Candia rugosa and Rhizopus niveus lipase. Porcine pancreas lipase manifested catalytic promiscuity by conversion of 4-hydroxycoumarin and aromatic aldehyde to Bis-4-hydroxycoumarin through Knoevenagel condensation; of aromatic or heteroaromatic aldehyde and ketone to aldol through aldol condensation. It outweighed lipases from Aspergillus niger, Pesudomonas fluorescens and Candia rugosa during Michael addition between 4-hydroxycoumarin and α, β-unsaturated enones to warfarin. It outperformed Mucor javanicus lipase during cascade reaction involving aldehyde and indole to Bis(indolyl)alkanes; and Candida cylindracea lipase during enantioselective acylation between amino alcohol and acetate ester to amide and amido-ester. This lipase also catalyzed multicomponent synthesis leading to Pyrido[2,3-d]pyrimidine derivatives from aromatic aldehyde, malononitrile and 6-amino-1,3-dimethyl uracil. This lipase has potential application value as it could catalyze these reactions under milder conditions.

papers.title: Discovery and characterization of a thermostable CALB-type lipase for efficient ethyl hexanoate synthesis in aqueous systems.
papers.abstractText: Candida antarctica lipase B (CALB) is a prototypical biocatalyst, distinguished by its remarkable catalytic efficiency in industrial ester synthesis. In this study, a novel lipase, XyEst, from Xylariales sp. PMI_506, was identified via the construction of a sequence similarity network and structural homology analysis using CALB as a reference. Despite sharing only 23.83% sequence identity with CALB, XyEst adopts a highly similar overall fold, indicating the presence of a conserved catalytic framework. The recombinant enzyme (rXyEst) displayed optimal activity at 30 °C and pH 4 for ethyl hexanoate synthesis. Notably, rXyEst exhibited remarkable thermal stability, retaining over 30% of its activity after 1 h at 70 °C. Furthermore, rXyEst showed strong tolerance to diverse metal ions and surfactants. In aqueous systems, rXyEst efficiently catalyzed ethyl hexanoate formation, achieving 65% conversion within 8 h. Collectively, these findings highlight XyEst as a thermostable biocatalyst with promising potential for sustainable industrial ester synthesis.

papers.title: Structure-guided engineering of medium- and long-chain triglycerides:​Fermentation-assisted biosynthesis, structural control and future perspective.
papers.abstractText: Medium- and long-chain triglycerides (MLCTs) are triacylglycerols (TAGs) that have medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs) and long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs) linked together on a single glycerol backbone. The positioning of the components, such as the MCFA-LCFA-MCFA (MLM-type) positioning, can affect lipase-mediated hydrolysis, release of fatty acids (FAs), absorption and metabolic behavior, however, structure-function relationships requires experimental validation. This review presents a comparison between chemical interesterification, lipase-catalyzed interesterification and fermentation-assisted biosynthesis of MLCT. Chemical interesterification will redistribute fatty acyl groups, but offers​ limited positional control, while lipase-catalyzed synthesis provides more positional selectivity but is susceptible to acyl migration. Fermentation-​assisted biosynthesis is a prospective approach that connects FA chain-length control, acyl-CoA supply and TAG assembly more strongly. However, there is currently more evidence that strongly supports the production of tailored FAs by microbes than demonstrated positional control of MLCT molecular species. Structural validation requires intact TAG molecular species analysis, positional analysis, and stereospecific analysis. An integrated framework combining applications of structural analysis, selective biocatalysis, fermentation optimization, metabolic engineering and functional evaluation is proposed.

papers.title: Breeding of high-yield low-temperature lipase fungi, optimization of fermentation conditions and isolation and purification of lipase
papers.abstractText: Abstract    The low-temperature lipase, due to its unique low-temperature adaptability and catalytic properties, has become a highly focused research hotspot in the field of enzymology, and the re-search around it has been continuously deepening. This study aims to efficiently produce a low-temperature lipase to address the problems of low activity, high cost, and limited application of common lipases under low-temperature conditions. During the research process, we collected samples from the natural environment at low temperatures, and through multiple rounds of screening, we obtained fungi with strong lipase production capabilities. We further enhanced their lipase production capacity through ultraviolet-uranine guanidine compound mutagenesis and optimization of fermentation conditions. Finally, we separated and purified the lipase using ammonium sulfate precipitation, Q-HP anion exchange chromatography, and Superdex 75 gel filtration chromatography, and determined its Lipaseology properties. The research results showed that a strain of Aspergillus niger was screened out. After mutagenesis treatment, the mutant strain increased the lipase production by 127.35%. On this basis, the lipase production was further improved to 57.26 U/mL under optimized fermentation conditions. The isolated low-temperature lipase had a specific activity of up to 113.52 U/mg. Its optimal reaction temperature was measured to be 30°C, and it still maintained over 60% activity at 15°C, which was higher than the low-temperature activity of common commercial lipases. The low-temperature lipase obtained in this study can be applied in food processing, low-temperature washing, and environmental governance, effectively reducing the energy consumption and operating costs of related industries. The related preparation methods can provide a scientific basis and feasible solutions for the large-scale production of low-temperature lipases.
